I'm not qualified to judge how "strong" these passwords are, but they're probably way stronger than "monkey" or "password123" or such. Copy the line below completely and paste into your terminal.

2> /dev/null dd if=/dev/random bs=1 count=21 | base64 | xsel -i

The xsel part just puts the password on your clipboard. If you want to print the password to the terminal, or if you don't have xsel, then do this:

 2> /dev/null dd if=/dev/random bs=1 count=21 | base64

If you want shorter passwords (why?), or longer passwords (good!), then change the count=21 part. It's the number of octets fetched from /dev/random. While it affects the password length, the generated password will always be longer because of base64 encoding.

 2> /dev/null dd if=/dev/random bs=1 count=30 | base64

Hope you all will appreciate this and share any improvements.

This is one I wrote forever ago to deal with broken accounts in a heavily-audited environment that checked for password rotation and lastlog:

#!/bin/bash
#
#Usage:
#Run as root!
#./spwlogin.sh username (password)
# Password is optional
#
#Logic:
#1. Reset user's password to random, 25-char string.
#2. Check if root has a public key.
# a. If yes, check if that key is in the user's authorized keys
# i. If not in authorized keys, append it.
# b. If root does not have a public key, create one, and append it to the
#user's authorized keys.
#3. SSH to localhost as user, using root's public key to authenticate, then
#exit.
#4. Echo to screen what has been done.

if [ "$1" = "" ] || [ `cat /etc/passwd | grep -c $1` -lt 1 ]; then
 echo "No or bad username provided. Exiting."
 exit 11
fi

if [ "$2" != "" ]; then
 PASS="$2"
else
 PASS=`</dev/urandom tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9-_!@#$%^&*+?=' | head -c25`
fi

echo "$PASS" | passwd --stdin $1

if [ -e /root/.ssh/id_rsa.pub ]; then
 if ! grep -q "`cat /root/.ssh/id_rsa.pub`" /home/$1/.ssh/authorized_keys
 then
 cat /root/.ssh/id_rsa.pub >> /home/$1/.ssh/authorized_keys
 fi
else
 echo ; echo ; echo | ssh-keygen -t rsa
 cat /root/.ssh/id_rsa.pub >> /home/$1/.ssh/authorized_keys
fi

echo exit | ssh -t -t -q $1@`hostname` >/dev/null 2>&1

if [ "$2" = "" ]; then
 echo Password for user $1 has been changed to:
 echo $PASS
fi

echo Last login date has been reset.

exit 0

If you want a one-liner, all the magic happens here:

</dev/urandom tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9-_!@#$%^&*+?=' | head -c25

Some remarks from me:

  • I don't know the implications of sourcing bits from /dev/urandom as opposed to /dev/random. Ask a crypto expert.
  • The tr -dc 'blabla...' bit is nice because it allows fine grained tuning of password characters, whereas my simple base64 is constrained to base64 valid symbols. Mine is easier to type, but less flexible. Choose which you prefer for your one-liner.
  • I could have simplified my one-liner by using head -c31, and I'll probably edit that into the OP.
